title: Jeremiah 32:16–25
context: Jeremiah 32:16–25 is Jeremiah’s prayer after giving the deed to Baruch. He praises the Lord GOD as the Creator for whom nothing is too hard, who shows loving kindness to thousands and repays iniquity, whose eyes see all human ways, and who brought Israel out of Egypt with signs and gave them the land promised to their fathers. Israel did not obey, so this disaster has come; siege ramps are against the city, and what God spoke has happened. Jeremiah ends with a question implied in his words: the LORD told him to buy a field, though the city is being given to the Chaldeans. Both traditions read the prayer as a model of faith that holds God’s power and justice together while honestly bringing a puzzle before him.

verses.text: Now after I had delivered the deed of the purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed to the LORD, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: After giving the deed to Baruch, Jeremiah prays to the LORD. Arminians see the prophet turning to prayer after obedience, bringing his questions to God rather than keeping them to himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see prayer as the natural response of faith when God’s ways are hard to understand. Both traditions read Jeremiah’s prayer as a model of honest dependence on God.

verses.text: “Ah Lord GOD! Behold, you have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm. There is nothing too hard for you.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah praises the Lord GOD who made the heavens and earth by his great power, and says nothing is too hard for him. Arminian readers see faith grounded in God’s power as Creator, which gives hope even when circumstances seem hopeless.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s power as the basis for trusting his promises. Both traditions compare Genesis 18:14 and note that the LORD himself takes up these words in 32:27.

verses.text: You show loving kindness to thousands, and repay the iniquity of the fathers into the bosom of their children after them. The great, the mighty God, the LORD of Armies is your name:
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says God shows loving kindness to thousands and repays the iniquity of fathers into the bosom of their children. Arminians see God’s character as both merciful and just, as revealed at Sinai (Exodus 20:5–6 and 34:6–7).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the same revelation of God’s name. Both traditions note that Jeremiah 31:29–30 and Ezekiel 18 address how each person bears responsibility, and they read this verse in harmony with those texts rather than as fatalism.

verses.text: great in counsel, and mighty in work; whose eyes are open to all the ways of the children of men, to give everyone according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings;
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah praises God as great in counsel and mighty in work, who sees all human ways and repays each according to his deeds. Arminian readers see God’s justice, which treats people according to their real choices and actions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s perfect knowledge and righteous judgment. Both traditions hold this as shared ground about God’s justice, and they note that it explains why the coming judgment on Jerusalem is fair.

verses.text: who performed signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, even to this day, both in Israel and among other men; and made yourself a name, as it is today;
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah recalls the signs and wonders God did in Egypt and since then, making a name for himself. Arminians see God’s past acts as the ground for trusting his future promises.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s mighty acts as revealing his glory. Both traditions read the verse as linking the exodus with God’s continuing work in Israel and among the nations.

verses.text: and brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs, with wonders, with a strong hand, with an outstretched arm, and with great terror;
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah recalls how God brought Israel out of Egypt with signs, wonders, a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and great terror. Arminian readers see the exodus as the great act of salvation that defined Israel’s relationship with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the language as echoing Deuteronomy’s descriptions of the exodus (compare Deuteronomy 26:8). Both traditions hold the exodus as shared ground about God’s redeeming power.

verses.text: and gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah recalls that God gave them the land he swore to their fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey. Arminians see God’s faithfulness to his promise to the patriarchs, which makes Israel’s later unfaithfulness more tragic.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s covenant faithfulness in giving the land. Both traditions note that the gift of the land is now about to be lost, which sets up the tension in Jeremiah’s prayer.

verses.text: They came in and possessed it, but they didn’t obey your voice and didn’t walk in your law. They have done nothing of all that you commanded them to do. Therefore you have caused all this evil to come upon them.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says they possessed the land but did not obey or walk in God’s law, so God brought this disaster. Arminian readers see judgment as the result of the people’s persistent disobedience, which God warned about for generations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as confessing the justice of God’s judgment. Both traditions hold that the exile is not arbitrary but follows from covenant unfaithfulness, as Deuteronomy 28 warned.

verses.text: “Behold, siege ramps have been built against the city to take it. The city is given into the hand of the Chaldeans who fight against it, because of the sword, of the famine, and of the pestilence. What you have spoken has happened. Behold, you see it.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says siege ramps are against the city and it is given to the Chaldeans through sword, famine, and pestilence, as God said. Arminians see the prophet acknowledging that God’s warnings have come true.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the fulfillment of God’s word in judgment. Both traditions read the closing words, Behold, you see it, as Jeremiah laying the situation before God, preparing for his question.

verses.text: You have said to me, Lord GOD, ‘Buy the field for money, and call witnesses;’ whereas the city is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says the Lord GOD told him to buy the field and call witnesses, though the city is being handed to the Chaldeans. Arminian readers see honest faith that obeys while still asking God to explain what seems contradictory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see Jeremiah bringing his puzzlement to God in prayer. Both traditions note that Jeremiah does not doubt God’s power, which he praised in verse 17, but asks how the promise fits the present disaster.
